passage:
"Arohi, why do you talk like that on the phone?"
"Like what, Indu?"
"All 'yaar' and 'chill' with your friends. With Nani you speak Marathi like a priest."
Arohi laughed. "Because Nani would faint if I said 'chill.'"
"So which one is the real you?"
Arohi stopped folding clothes. She thought about it. "Both?" she said. "At school I used to hide the Marathi. Someone laughed at my accent in Class 7."
"And now?"
"Now I taught three girls the Marathi word for 'annoying.' They use it all the time."
Indu grinned. "What is it?"
"I'm not telling you. You'll use it on me."
"Aai says you sound like her when you're angry."
Arohi smiled. "Good."

qa.q: What did Arohi teach three girls at school?
qa.a: She taught them the Marathi word for "annoying."

qa.q: What does Arohi's "Good" at the end suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she's proud of sounding like her mother and now feels comfortable with her home language rather than ashamed of it.

qa.q: What helped Arohi move from hiding her Marathi to sharing it?
qa.a: Sharing a fun word with friends turned her language into something others enjoyed, instead of something to be laughed at.

qa.q: How might Indu see her older sister's switching between languages?
qa.a: She seems curious and slightly teasing, but she also learns that switching can be natural, not fake.

grounding: It shows a teen moving between home, school and friend language with growing pride instead of shame.

passage: When I moved from Kochi to Delhi in Class 8, I stopped speaking Malayalam outside the house. I'm Joseph. At my new school, a boy imitated my accent in the canteen, and everyone laughed. So I copied the way the Delhi boys talked, their slang, the way they said "bhai." At home, Amma would ask me something in Malayalam and I'd answer in Hindi. She never said anything, but I saw her face. Then last year my friend Lalit came over for lunch. Amma made appam and stew. Lalit ate three and begged for the recipe. He asked me to teach him Malayalam words. I felt proud, and weirdly relieved. Now I switch without thinking much. Different rooms, different voices, same me.

qa.q: What did Amma make when Lalit came for lunch?
qa.a: She made appam and stew.

qa.q: What might Amma have felt when Joseph answered her in Hindi?
qa.a: She may have felt hurt or sad that her son seemed to be pulling away from their language, though she didn't say it.

qa.q: What helped Joseph feel proud of his heritage again?
qa.a: Seeing a friend enjoy his mother's food and want to learn Malayalam showed him his culture could be admired, not mocked.

qa.q: How might Lalit see Joseph's switching between languages?
qa.a: He probably sees it as interesting and even cool, a sign that Joseph belongs in more than one world.

grounding: A teen reflects on hiding his home language after mockery and regaining pride while switching between cultures.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Class 10:
Kashish asked to see me after an incident in the class group chat. She had posted a photo from her cousin's wedding, wearing a traditional outfit, and someone commented, "Village vibes." She deleted the photo. In our session she said she felt like two people: one at home with Punjabi songs and big family dinners, one at school trying to seem "cool." I asked what she liked about each. She smiled about the dinners.
We talked about how moving between groups is normal, and how she could choose what to share. Her friend Keerthana, from another state, told her she loved the photo.
Follow-up: Kashish reposted it with the caption "My people." I've told the class teacher about the comment.

qa.q: What caption did Kashish use when she reposted the photo?
qa.a: She used the caption "My people."

qa.q: How did Kashish feel after the "Village vibes" comment?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and split, like two different people, which is why she deleted the photo.

qa.q: What in the counsellor's approach helped Kashish?
qa.a: Asking what she liked about each part of her life, and saying moving between groups is normal, helped her feel she didn't have to hide one side.

qa.q: How might Keerthana's comment have affected Kashish?
qa.a: Hearing that a friend loved the photo probably made her feel accepted and gave her courage to repost it. 🙂

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a teen moving from shame to pride about her home culture after an online comment.

passage:
Friday
Today in the corridor, Rakesh copied the way I say 'school' and three people laughed. I wanted the floor to swallow me. At home I speak Marathi with Aaji, at school I try to sound like the English channels, and online I talk in memes. Three Omkars. Sometimes I don't know which Omkar is real.
In the evening Aaji was making thalipeeth, and I filmed her hands, just because. Then Tushar texted, 'Post it, my mom will want the recipe.' So I did, a short video, Aaji talking in Marathi with English subtitles I typed. By night it had comments from people in Pune and even Dubai saying 'this is my Aaji too'.
Maybe all three Omkars are real. Maybe that's okay.

qa.q: What was Aaji making when Omkar filmed her?
qa.a: Thalipeeth.

qa.q: What did Omkar feel when Rakesh copied the way Omkar said 'school'?
qa.a: Embarrassed and ashamed, wishing the floor would swallow them.

qa.q: What helped Omkar feel prouder of Omkar's home culture?
qa.a: Sharing Aaji's recipe in Marathi with subtitles and seeing others connect with it warmly.

qa.q: How might Aaji feel if she saw the comments on the video?
qa.a: She would likely be delighted and touched that strangers loved her cooking and language.

grounding: A teen writes about moving between home, school and online cultures and finding pride instead of shame.

passage: On the evening bus from Kotdwar to her village, Usha finally opened her video. Twenty seconds: her Dadi's hands shaping mandua rotis, Usha's voice explaining in Garhwali, then the same line in English. Bhupen, squeezed beside her with a sack of rice, leaned over. "Garhwali? Online? The town girls will laugh." At school Usha spoke careful English and Hindi; at home, Garhwali came without thinking. For months she had kept them apart like two dupattas folded in different trunks. She looked at the comments. A stranger had written, "My nani says this word too!" Another asked what mandua was. "Let them laugh," Usha said, surprised at how steady she sounded. "Some are asking." Bhupen read the comment twice, then said quietly, "Do the next one on Dadi's pickle."

qa.q: What were Dadi's hands shaping in Usha's video?
qa.a: Mandua rotis.

qa.q: What was Usha feeling when she answered Bhupen?
qa.a: Usha felt a quiet pride, and some surprise at her own steadiness, after months of keeping her languages apart.

qa.q: What could help Usha keep moving between her languages without shame?
qa.a: Usha could keep pairing Garhwali with English as in the video, and pay attention to the curious comments rather than the imagined laughter.

qa.q: Why might Bhupen react differently by the end of the ride?
qa.a: The stranger recognising the word and others asking questions showed Bhupen that the language draws interest, so the teasing turned into a request for more.

grounding: A village teenager shares a video in her home language and stops hiding it from school and online worlds.

passage: At the corner table of the school cafeteria in Toronto, Rosa's phone buzzed with a voice note from her avó. She thumbed the volume down to nothing. Her avó's Portuguese was loud and warm and full of kisses, and last year someone had mimicked it for a week. Yara, unwrapping stuffed grape leaves, noticed. "You never play them." "It's embarrassing." Yara shrugged, pressed her own phone, and her teta's Arabic filled the table, asking whether Yara had eaten. A boy at the next table glanced up, then went back to his fries. "See?" Yara said. "Nobody fainted." Rosa laughed, lifted the phone to her ear and answered in Portuguese, quietly at first, then less quietly. That afternoon in English class she was the same Rosa who argued about poems. Both voices, she thought, were hers.

qa.q: In which city is Rosa's school?
qa.a: Toronto.

qa.q: Why did Rosa turn the volume down to nothing?
qa.a: Rosa felt embarrassed, because last year someone had mimicked her avó's loud Portuguese, and she feared being mocked again.

qa.q: What did Yara's example show, and how could Rosa build on it?
qa.a: Yara showed that playing a family voice note openly caused no disaster; Rosa could keep answering in Portuguese at lunch and let her confidence grow.

qa.q: How might Rosa's avó feel hearing Rosa answer from the cafeteria?
qa.a: Rosa's avó would likely feel delighted and close to Rosa, hearing Portuguese answered in the middle of a school day.

grounding: A teenager in Canada stops muting her grandmother's language at school after a friend plays her own.

passage: Heritage Day was a week away, and the hostel common room buzzed with plans. Sahil had signed up for "something funny", maybe a meme skit in the slang everyone used online. Then his mother called and sang, off-key, the Konkani boat song his grandfather used to hum while mending nets. After the call Sahil sat still, phone warm in his hand. Suraj looked down from the top bunk. "That's the song? Teach me." "It's old. People will think it's weird." "You do three accents a day, bro. English for Sir, Hindi for the mess uncle, meme voice for us. Add one." On Heritage Day Sahil sang the first verse alone, voice shaking, then Suraj joined the chorus he had practised badly all week. The juniors clapped along, and one asked Sahil to write the words down.

qa.q: Who used to hum the Konkani boat song?
qa.a: Sahil's grandfather, while mending nets.

qa.q: What might Sahil have been worried about before Heritage Day?
qa.a: Sahil was nervous that people would find the old song weird next to the easy meme skit everyone expected.

qa.q: How did Suraj help, and what could a teacher add?
qa.a: Suraj pointed out that Sahil already switches voices all day and then joined the chorus; a teacher could invite such songs through the year, not only on one day.

qa.q: How might the juniors see Sahil after the song?
qa.a: The juniors clearly enjoyed it and got curious, as one asked for the words, so Sahil probably looked brave and interesting to them.

grounding: A hostel student shares his family's Konkani song after a friend points out he already moves between many voices.

passage:
Dear Ishita,
You asked how I deal with switching between worlds. Honestly, it used to be hard.
At home, it's Tamil with Paati, and her kolam every morning. At school, it's English, and some boys used to laugh when I said "aiyo". Online, it's memes and slang I'd never say at home.
For a year I stopped speaking Tamil outside the house. Then at the school cultural fest, I did a Tamil poem with my friend Rohit playing the mridangam. People went silent, then clapped for ages.
Now I switch without shame. I'm one person with three languages, not three people. Paati says my Tamil is getting better, and my English essays are too.
Come visit in Pongal. Paati will feed you till you burst.
Anand

qa.q: What did Anand do at the school cultural fest?
qa.a: A Tamil poem, with Rohit playing the mridangam.

qa.q: What was Anand feeling during the year of not speaking Tamil outside?
qa.a: Anand felt ashamed and self-conscious after being laughed at.

qa.q: What helped Anand start switching without shame?
qa.a: Performing the Tamil poem and seeing people's respect showed that heritage could be a source of pride.

qa.q: How might Paati see Anand's change?
qa.a: Paati is likely proud and happy that Anand embraces Tamil again.

grounding: A teen writes to a cousin about moving between home, school and online cultures without shame.

passage:
So you want the story of my accent. I'm Vinita, and I grew up speaking Bhojpuri in a small town in Bihar. When I moved to a Delhi school in Class 9, a girl imitated me in front of the class. Everyone laughed.
After that, I practised "proper" Hindi and English every night. At home, I spoke Bhojpuri; at school, I went silent.
Then, in Class 10, our teacher asked us to present a folk song. My friend Dhruv said, "Do a Bhojpuri one. Nobody else can."
I was terrified. But I sang a song my Nani used to sing. The class went quiet. The same girl who laughed asked me to teach her the chorus.
That day I stopped hiding. I switch languages now, but I don't switch who I am.

qa.q: Who said "Do a Bhojpuri one"?
qa.a: Dhruv.

qa.q: What was Vinita feeling after being imitated in class?
qa.a: Vinita felt ashamed and hurt, hiding the accent and going silent at school.

qa.q: What choice inside the story turned things around for Vinita?
qa.a: Choosing to sing Vinita's Nani's Bhojpuri song in class showed that heritage as a strength.

qa.q: How might the girl who laughed have felt when she asked to learn the chorus?
qa.a: The girl probably felt respect and maybe some regret about the earlier mockery.

grounding: A young person tells how Vinita moved from hiding a dialect to switching languages with pride.

passage:
I'm Madhuri, and Nirmala sits next to me. On Heritage Day she came in a mekhela chador, the Assamese outfit her grandmother made.
At first she kept tugging at it and looking at the floor. Some boys whispered.
When it was her turn to speak, she started in English about Bihu. Then she switched to Assamese for the lines of a song, and back to English to explain them. Her voice got stronger as she went.
Afterwards, a boy asked her something in slang, and she answered in the same slang, laughing.
I don't know what she was feeling at the start. By the end, she was standing up very straight.

qa.q: What did Nirmala wear on Heritage Day?
qa.a: A mekhela chador, the Assamese outfit her grandmother made.

qa.q: What might Nirmala have been feeling when she tugged at her outfit?
qa.a: Nirmala was probably self-conscious and nervous about being different.

qa.q: How could teachers support students like Nirmala on days like this?
qa.a: Teachers could welcome all languages and outfits and step in if anyone mocks, so students feel safe to share.

qa.q: How does Madhuri see Nirmala by the end?
qa.a: Madhuri isn't sure how Nirmala felt at first but sees her standing tall and proud by the end.

grounding: A classmate watches a teen move confidently between Assamese, English and slang on Heritage Day.

passage:
Monday: Farhan's mother came to school to drop his forgotten tiffin and called out across the corridor in Dakhni, "Arre, Farhan, khana bhool gaye kya?" A few boys copied her accent. Farhan grabbed the tiffin and walked off fast, face burning.
Wednesday: Kalyani found him on the stairs. "You speak three languages, you know. Dakhni at home, English here, and whatever that is in your gaming chats."
"The home one's the embarrassing one."
"I switch too. Telugu with Ammamma, English with teachers, Hindi with you. It's not embarrassing. It's a skill."
Friday: For language day, the teacher asked everyone to teach a phrase from home. Farhan hesitated, then taught "kaiku?" (why?) and showed how his mother says it with her hands. The class laughed, but this time with him. Two boys used it all afternoon.

qa.q: What phrase did Farhan teach on language day?
qa.a: He taught "kaiku?", meaning "why?".

qa.q: Why did Farhan walk off fast on Monday?
qa.a: Farhan felt embarrassed and ashamed when the boys mocked his mother's accent.

qa.q: What helped Farhan move from shame to pride?
qa.a: Kalyani's idea that switching languages is a skill, and the language day that gave him a chance to share his home language on his own terms.

qa.q: How might Farhan's mother feel if she heard the class using "kaiku?"
qa.a: His mother would probably feel proud and touched that her way of speaking was being celebrated.

grounding: Shows a teen over several days moving from shame to pride about switching between home, school and online languages.

passage:
Sachin, you think your accent will make them laugh at college? Let me tell you mine.
When I was sixteen, I came from our village near Chhapra to a hostel in Mumbai. The first day I said "hum" for "I", and the boys in my room laughed till they cried. So I stopped talking. For months I practised "main" in the mirror. When Maa called, I whispered Bhojpuri so nobody would hear.
Then at the hostel's cultural night, a senior sang a Bhojpuri folk song. The whole hall clapped. After, he came to me: "You're from Saran? Talk to me in our language, yaar, I miss it."
I realised I'd been hiding the thing I was proud of at home. Now I speak English at the office, Hindi with friends, Bhojpuri with Maa, loudly. Your Nitin Chacha changes languages ten times a day and is ashamed of none.

qa.q: What did the senior sing at the cultural night?
qa.a: A Bhojpuri folk song.

qa.q: How did young Nitin feel whispering Bhojpuri on the phone to Maa?
qa.a: Young Nitin felt ashamed and afraid of being laughed at, so he hid the language he loved.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Nitin's story, and why?
qa.a: The senior asking to speak Bhojpuri with him, because it showed his home language could be something to share, not hide.

qa.q: How might the senior have felt meeting young Nitin?
qa.a: The senior was probably homesick and delighted to find someone from the same region to speak with.

grounding: Illustrates an elder recalling how he moved from hiding his home language to switching proudly between cultures.

passage:
Yash was forty minutes into a live gaming stream with his friend Parveen, two hundred people watching, when his Ba walked in with a plate of thepla.
"Yash, khaai le, beta. Thandu thai jashe."
The chat exploded: "lol what language", "grandma cameo", "subtitles pls". Yash's ears went red. The game was at a crucial point; he had seconds to decide what to do.
He took the plate. "Thank you, Ba." Then, to the camera: "That's Gujarati. My Ba says eat before it gets cold. She's the real boss here."
Parveen laughed. "Ba, say hi!"
Ba waved at the screen, confused and delighted. The chat filled with "hi Ba", and someone asked for the thepla recipe.
After the stream Yash sat for a moment. He had expected to be mocked. Instead the clip with Ba got the most views.

qa.q: What did Yash's Ba bring into the room?
qa.a: A plate of thepla.

qa.q: What was Yash feeling when the chat exploded?
qa.a: Yash felt embarrassed, with red ears, and worried he'd be mocked on stream.

qa.q: Which choice turned the moment around, and why?
qa.a: Explaining Ba's words proudly instead of hiding her made the moment warm, so viewers joined in rather than mocking.

qa.q: How might Ba see the moment?
qa.a: Ba was confused but delighted, probably happy to be greeted by her grandson's friends online.

grounding: Shows a teen switching between home language and online culture live, choosing pride over embarrassment.

passage: Sarika's phone buzzed with the group chat, all lowercase slang and memes, while her mother called from the kitchen in Assamese: "Sarika, pitha khabi?" Two classmates sat at the dining table colouring a geography map, and one of them, Bhupen, looked up. Last year Sarika would have answered in quick Hindi and pretended not to hear the rest. Her cheeks still warmed a little. This time she called back in Assamese, then turned to the table. "She's asking if we want pitha. Rice cakes. My grandmother's recipe." Bhupen said, "Wait, say that again?" and tried the word, badly. Sarika laughed and corrected him, twice. Later she typed in the chat, "ok the pitha was elite," and switched back to English for the map legend without thinking twice about any of it.

qa.q: What were Sarika and her classmates working on at the dining table?
qa.a: They were colouring a geography map.

qa.q: How can you tell Sarika still felt a little self-conscious about speaking Assamese in front of classmates?
qa.a: Her cheeks warmed and she remembered hiding it in Hindi last year, so some embarrassment was still there, but pride won and she answered in Assamese anyway.

qa.q: What made the moment go well, and what could Sarika keep doing?
qa.a: She explained the word simply and let Bhupen try it, turning her home language into something to share; she can keep switching languages openly instead of hiding one.

qa.q: How does Bhupen see Sarika's home language?
qa.a: He seems curious rather than mocking, since he asks her to repeat the word and tries to say it himself 🙂

grounding: Illustrates a teen moving between home, school and online language easily and showing pride in her heritage.
